class_id: a test asserts a rule the codebase deliberately removed
feature: any validation threshold, guard or business rule that was removed on purpose, and the tests written against it while it existed
symptom: a test fails because the code no longer enforces something it once did, and the removal was CORRECT. The failure looks identical to a regression, so the obvious repair — change the code until the test passes — REINSTATES the removed bug. The tell is a test whose docstring or comment cites a specific constant or rule as ground truth ("min=10 per field-priority-matrix") while the code carries a dated comment explaining why that constant was deleted. Universal shape: when a rule is removed, its tests are a second, independent copy of the rule, and nothing links the two, so the removal is complete in the code and silent in the tests. The danger is asymmetric: a stale test read as a regression produces a real product defect, while a stale test read correctly costs one edit.
first_seen: 2026-09-20 — issue #832 / PR #836. `web/tests/integration/data-flow/lot-size-validation.integration.test.ts` (2 tests) asserted that a lot size below 10 is rejected, citing "min=10 per field-priority-matrix" in its own docstring. The matrix carries `lot_size: validation: { min: 1, max: 100000 }` with a dated comment at `field-priority-matrix.ts:566` recording the deletion as deliberate: "`min: 10` here was a SECOND, silently-enforced copy of the 'legal minimum lot' rule (SEBI sets no universal floor — a high-priced issue can legally have a lot under 10 shares, e.g. lot=8 at a band of ~1700-1785). `validateValue` only ever sees the bare number, never the price band, so it cannot tell a legitimate high-price lot from garbage." Reinstating the floor to satisfy the test would have rejected legitimate high-price IPOs. Found only because PR #834 fixed a harness gap that had been masking these two failures among twelve
fix_prs: #836 corrects the TEST to the matrix's real floor (rejection case `lot_size=0`, boundary case `lot_size=1`), leaving the production rule as the deliberate removal left it. The general remedy is the classification step, not this edit: every failing test is triaged as (a) product bug, (b) test-setup gap, or (c) stale test BEFORE any code is changed, and a (c) is fixed test-side only
detection_check: none yet, and a mechanical one is hard: nothing links a removed constant to the tests that asserted it. What is cheap and would have caught this: when a validation threshold is deleted, grep the test tree for the literal value and the field name in the same change, and treat any hit as part of the removal. A review question that generalises: 'if this test is failing, would fixing the CODE to satisfy it re-introduce something a dated comment says was removed on purpose?' Note that `config/web-integration-baseline.json` recorded this file as failing for ten days without anyone asking which of the three classes it was — a shrink-only list with no triage behind its entries hides exactly this
